zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after reading the scan: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription corrections and English review notes here are this review's scan-based work, not a replacement transcription supplied by NINJAL.

lines.note: Miuo completes Su- from the preceding page, giving sumi wo suri, suru, grinding ink. The next example begins sumi wo again; Moertinta retains the printed spacing.

runs.text: Tingir algũa couſa de preto por cima

lines.note: Sumi wo nuru means coating something with ink, here coloring its surface black. The instrument is supplied by the following continuation.
The black coating is applied with a brush. This short line is visibly indented like the preceding continuation, not aligned as a new entry.
This sumi is charcoal, distinct from ink. Sumi wo yaku means making charcoal by burning wood; the Portuguese sentence continues below.
After completing the charcoal-making gloss, sumi wo okosu introduces kindling a charcoal fire. The historical spelling vocoſu is retained.
Sumi wo tsugu is feeding or replenishing charcoal. The Portuguese ceuã- begins the verb for feeding the fire.
The fire is fed with charcoal. Sumi ga nadaruru then begins the contrasting example of the charcoal fire dying down.
Ru completes nadaruru. The Portuguese describes the fire gradually going out and turning to ash, rather than simply being extinguished at once.
The delayed subject is the charcoal fire. This closes the sequence of examples under charcoal, before the separate corner sense.

runs.text: Canto da caſa, ou de outra couſa diuidi-

lines.note: Sumi now means a corner of a house or another object. The divided Portuguese word continues the geometric description below.

runs.text: da em quatro partes, ou mais.

lines.note: The object is described as divided into four or more parts. This completes the historical corner definition without substituting a modern geometric formulation.
Sumiaka no hako is a small box for women's cosmetics or adornments. The scan supports no faco rather than the draft's malformed ſio faco.
Feites completes afeites, women's adornments or cosmetics. This is still the contents of the small box, not another Japanese entry.
Sumiarashi means letting one's dwelling deteriorate through neglect. The visible m restores the headword; aita is retained as its historical principal-part ending.

runs.text: a caſa em que hum mora por não a concertar, nẽ

lines.note: The house falls into disrepair because its resident does not mend it. Concertar retains the source's spelling for putting things in order.
Ie wo sumi-arasu illustrates neglecting the house one occupies. The printed separation in ſumi araſu is retained rather than joined from morphological expectation.
Sumibi is a charcoal fire, a transparent compound matching the short Portuguese gloss.
Sumika means a dwelling or habitation. The scan supports the initial h in habitação, correcting OCR babitação.
This sumikane describes a reason or dispute failing to be settled. The negative Portuguese gloss distinguishes it from a successfully concluded matter.
Zão completes razão; a lawsuit or dispute is the alternative object. The line closes the unresolved-matter sense.
The homonymous sumikane means having difficulty remaining or living somewhere. Its relation to residence distinguishes it from the preceding settlement sense.
This completes dificuldade em algum lugar, difficulty living in a particular place. It remains a continuation of the preceding verb entry.
Sumi kane names the carpenter's ink and square. The printed terminal mark after carpintei is retained rather than silently converted into a conventional hyphen.
Ro completes carpinteiro. Sumi kane wo atsuru illustrates applying the ink and square; the scan restores caneuo rather than OCR caieuo.
The carpenter uses the square and ink for taking measurements. This closes the example under sumi kane.
Sumichigiri is referred to the preferred sumikiri, becoming completely clear. The scan restores the headword and itta; Meliùs is wholly italic Latin apparatus.

runs.text: Aclararſe muito, ou de todo agoa, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The definition is water becoming very or entirely clear. The printed sequence de todo agoa is retained without supplying an extra article.
Mizu ga sumichigitta illustrates water that has cleared completely. The upright final B marks low-register usage according to the supplied key.

runs.text: Lugar q̃ ſe habita, ou morada.

lines.note: Sumidokoro is a place where one lives, or a dwelling. Lugar corrects OCR Ligar, while the abbreviated q̃ remains unexpanded.
Sumihate, sumihatsuru refers to remaining resident somewhere to the end of one's life. The Portuguese locative phrase continues below.
Completes lugar atè a morte: living in that place until death. The endpoint is essential to the compound's meaning.

runs.text: Caruão não bem queimado que fu-

lines.note: Sumigashira is incompletely burned charcoal that smokes when put on a fire. The damaged m is restored rather than retaining Sunigaxira.

runs.text: mega quando ſe poem no fogo.

lines.note: Mega completes fumega, 'smokes', and the condition is being placed on the fire. This explains the charcoal's incomplete charring.

runs.text: Traues q̃ ſaem fora nos cãtos da caſa.

lines.note: Sumigi denotes beams projecting at the corners of a house. Both q̃ and cãtos retain the printed nasal or abbreviation marks.
Suminare means becoming accustomed to living somewhere. The source's acuſtumado is retained rather than modernized.
Rar completes morar and the habituation concerns residence in a particular place, not familiarity with a person.
Sumikirazu refers to fully square trays or tables, equated here with oshiki. The definition emphasizes corners that have not been cut off.

runs.text: todo, ou que não ſão rombas nos cantos.

lines.note: The corners are not blunted or rounded. Rombas, with b, corrects OCR romhas and explains the negative kirazu in the headword.

runs.text: Hũa erua aßi chamada cuja raiz he

lines.note: This sumire is a herb with an edible root. The scan reads erua rather than erus; the root comparison follows below.
The root resembles garlic and is eaten. This historical identification should not be conflated automatically with every modern plant called sumire.
A second sumire is simply named as a flower. The separate entry is preserved rather than merged with the edible-root definition.
Sumisashi is the carpenter's ink-marking pen. The Portuguese pena denotes the writing or marking implement here.
Sumitsubo is the carpenter's ink container or inking tool, explained literally as the carpenters' inkwell.
Sumiwabi describes living somewhere with weariness or distress. The Portuguese divides enfadamento across this and the next line.

runs.text: mento, ou tristeza em algum lugar.

lines.note: Weariness and sadness characterize residence in that place, completing the emotional sense of the preceding compound verb.
Sumiwatari means becoming very clear or clear throughout. The objects clarified are explicitly supplied in the following continuation.

runs.text: por todas as partes a agoa, ar, &c.

lines.note: Both water and air can become clear throughout. The scan restores todas as partes and the omitted ar, which the draft had obscured.
Sumiyakana describes something swift or prompt; the dictionary also supplies a clear or lucid sense in the continuation.
After the clarity sense, sumiyakana hito illustrates a prompt, efficient person. This continuation is indented in the scan.
Homem is completed across the break, and the person is diligent and efficient. The row shares the continuation indentation.
Sumiyakani is the corresponding adverb, 'swiftly' or 'promptly'. The print provides no separate Portuguese gloss, so none is added to the canonical text.
Sumiyakasa is the nominal derivative, swiftness or promptness. Its separate short physical row is retained without inventing an omitted definition.
Sumiyaki is a charcoal burner or charcoal maker, matching the occupational Portuguese carvoeiro in its printed spelling.

runs.text: Pintura de agoada de tinta preta.

lines.note: Sumi-e is painting with a wash of black ink. The Portuguese description explicitly concerns ink wash rather than coloring a surface solid black.
Sumizome is explained through a black outer garment worn by Buddhist clergy. The relative clause continues below.
Bonzos are the wearers of the outer garment. Sumizome no koromo gives the Japanese expression; Bõzos is an upright Portuguese borrowing here, not an embedded Japanese form to flag.
Idem assigns the same black-robe meaning to the preceding Japanese expression. It is a complete short continuation, not omitted text.
Sumizu is introduced through sumizu wo tsuku and the alternative awasuru. These concern squaring or aligning corners, explained below.

runs.text: Pondo a eſquadra, ou regra em al-

lines.note: Awasuru is completed across the break. The carpenter places a square or straightedge against an object with corners to align it.

runs.text: gũa obra de cantos, ou eſquinas endireitala,

lines.note: The object has corners or angles; the purpose is to straighten it. Gũa completes algũa from the preceding physical row.

runs.text: ou proporcionala de maneira que não ſaya hum

lines.note: The work is proportioned or aligned so that no one corner projects too far. The negative condition continues below.
After completing the literal corner-alignment sense, the entry introduces a figurative use of sumizu, divided after Sumiz-.

runs.text: Ser muito miudo em notar o q̃

lines.note: Figurative sumizu wo tsuku means scrutinizing what others do with excessive minuteness. The scan supports o q̃, not the OCR's osq̃.

runs.text: os outros fazem, tachando qualquer faltinha,

lines.note: The scrutiny becomes fault-finding, criticizing every small defect in other people's actions. Faltinha carries the diminutive force explicitly.
Sumizu wo tsuku hito applies the expression to a person. The Portuguese homem is divided at the physical break.
The person is excessively exacting and minute, not merely diligent. The long ſ in demaſiadamente corrects the draft's j.
The excessive exactness concerns noticing and criticizing the work of others. This closes the figurative woodworking metaphor.
Sumoo is wrestling, with sumoo wo toru meaning to wrestle. The scan has Sumǒuo without the draft's intrusive a.

runs.text: O tornar de balde ſem achar o que

lines.note: Sumodori is returning empty-handed or fruitlessly, not finding what one sought. The relative clause continues below.
The unsuccessful search is completed by buscava. Sumodori suru expresses performing that fruitless return, with Idem reusing the gloss.

runs.text: Certa laya de ameixias, ou amei-

lines.note: Sumomo is a kind of plum or plum tree. The source gives both fruit and tree, dividing the second Portuguese noun across the line break.
Completes ameixieiras, the alternative referring to the trees rather than just their plum-like fruit; the two-line division is retained.

runs.text: Medida de meo dedo indice que he o eſpã-

lines.note: Sun is explained by a bodily measure, half the index finger. The worn letter in Medida is d, not the draft's l; the nasal abbreviation and terminal division remain printed.

runs.text: ço dantre os dous nòs do meyo. Vt,

lines.note: The measure is the space between the two middle finger joints. The cedilla completes eſpãço; the example Iſſun has two long-s forms, not the draft's dotted i before ſ.
Niſun follows the one-sun example with two sun. A second sense is measurement generally, introducing the expression Sunuo toru across the line break.
Completes Sunuo toru and gives its Portuguese equivalent, to take a measurement; this short continuation is not another entry.
Suna is sand; Area is the historical Portuguese spelling here and is not expanded to modern areia.
Sunadori can denote fishing or a fisherman. The Japanese expression beginning Su- continues on the next physical row.
Completes Sunadoriuo ſuru, to fish. The divided Japanese word and italic Portuguese infinitive remain distinct.

runs.text: Area preta de que fazem ferro

lines.note: Sunagane is the black sand from which iron is made. The scan supports Area, not Atca; no terminal point is supplied where the line shows none.
Sunago first means sand, then a sprinkling of gold or silver. The second sense begins here and the word ouro continues on the next row.

runs.text: ro, ou de prata moida à maneira de area ſe-

lines.note: The precious metal is ground and scattered like sand. Moida has no visible nasal mark; the separate following à bears the accent. The final ſe- continues into ſemeada.
Completes ſemeada and introduces folding screens decorated with this metallic sprinkling. The Portuguese borrowing Biǒbus, like biǒbu, shows a small angular mark over o rather than the draft's tilde.
The screens are sprinkled with gold or silver. Suna- starts the next compound but remains on this physical row.

runs.text: O Salpicar, ou ſemear de ouro,

lines.note: Completes Sunagodami, the act of sprinkling or sowing gold; the Portuguese definition continues with silver on the following row.
Completes the gold-or-silver definition and gives a verbal expression of the same meaning. The printed space in Sunago damiuo is retained rather than harmonized with the headword.
Sunauachi is labelled an adverb and glossed as immediately or really. The punctuation after realmente is a semicolon in the scan, not the draft's comma.

runs.text: Couſa recta, ou inteira como ley,

lines.note: Sunauona describes something upright or sound, with law as the first example. The historical spelling is preserved rather than modernized to a current Japanese form.
Government completes the institutional examples; Sunauona fito applies the quality to a person, whose Portuguese description starts with divided Homem.
Completes the description of an upright, honest person, not a separate sense or headword.
The adverb corresponding to Sunauona is Sunauoni. The scan reads auo in the middle, not the draft's ato; only the grammatical label is printed as its explanation.

Sunbiô, with the Japanese paraphrase Sunno naye, refers to newly sprouted rice. The b is worn; its lower bowl and the lexical sequence support retaining the supplied headword, including its circumflex.

runs.text: uo de altura de meo dedo.

lines.note: Completes novo and specifies seedlings half a finger high, tying their height to the unit sun used in the surrounding entries.
Sunbun is explained through half-finger and tenth-part measures; the definition continues on the next page. The separate lower-margin parte is a catchword, not another body row.
